newsitem.title: CROATIA: US aid helps launch independent weekly in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: US aid helps launch independent weekly in Croatia.

text.p: An independent news magazine was launched in Croatia with U.S. financing on Friday to broaden free speech in a country where state-run media inclined to nationalist propaganda still predominate.

"The war is over in Croatia so the time has come for serious high-quality journalism," said Slavko Goldstein, managing director of Tjednik (Weekly) and a longtime human rights activist in the former Yugoslav republic.

"We will bring information to the public, not promote an ideology or fight for causes. We will be critical of the government, but we will not be an 'opposition' publication," he told a news conference unveiling the weekly.

Tjednik, whose editors include alumni of Croatia's first independent weekly harassed into extinction by autocratic authorities in 1992, resembles major Western news magazines in its punchy format and plentiful colour photography.

Goldstein told Reuters Tjednik received $500,000 in crucial start-up capital from the U.S. government's Agency for International Development (USAID) and several west European foundations, but hoped to be self-financing in a few months.
Goldstein said the weekly could break even with 50,000 circulation but would aim for 45,000 initially. Its cover price is 12 kuna ($3), relatively cheap by Croatian standards.

Tjednik's inaugural issue had seven pages of advertising spliced into 77 pages of sections on domestic and international politics and business, countries in transition (mainly east European like Croatia), and culture.
The magazine will be dedicated to news and analysis on Croatia and Bosnia, where a large Croat minority lives.

The lead article focused on Croat-Moslem violence in the divided Bosnian city of Mostar, concluding that Croats were to blame but this was covered up by nationalist disinformation spread by Croatia's mainstream media, especially television.

Goldstein said Tjednik's founders conducted market surveys showing there was considerable demand for a reliable newsmagazine that eschewed the sensationalism and half-truths characteristic of Croatia's independent tabloid press.
Tjednik's editor-in-chief is Krsto (Chris) Cviic, a liberal Croatian emigre and prominent Balkans scholar.
Cviic said that Tjednik would have no trouble countering possible HDZ accusations of hostile "foreign interference".
"There have been no secret deals. The Americans have helped us get started but no political strings are attached."

A state monopoly on media distribution outlets has been used to curb or prevent circulation of critical publications in the past. But Goldstein said Tjednik had signed an agreement with the Tisa monopoly assuring it would be distributed.

President Franjo Tudjman, an authoritarian nationalist, and powerful rightists in his HDZ party have hounded independent media for years despite Croatia's democratic constitution which guarantees freedom of the press.
But diplomats say Tudjman's room for preying on critical media has narrowed since Croatia was admitted to the Council of Europe, antechamber of the European Union, in October.
A month later, HDZ rightists tried to shut down Zagreb's popular Radio 101 on legal technicalities but backed off when 100,000 protesters hit the streets of the capital.
Cviic, in an introductory editorial, said Tjednik wanted to help Croatia emerge from "self-imposed" nationalist isolation.

"Croatia, as a young member of the club of sovereign countries, needs to know more about itself and the world," he wrote. "Although Croatia is now swarming with foreigners in all walks of life, it remains in many ways isolated from the world, very often because of the ways of those governing it.
"This is dangerous. It makes harder the very complex process of integration into the European Union and NATO."
